This game is a letdown. My review will consider The Last Door Season 2 as a sequel to the first season and not a stand-alone game.

Graphically, it's the same as TL1, but slightly better. Just a little bit. The art style is good, but the graphics just can't deliver it, unfortunately.

I'd like to talk about the two things that makes this game a letdown.

First: The imagery. It's weak, very weak.

You have the basic, shadow humanoid monsters, huge eyes, crows, fog, and that's basically it. That's acceptable for the first game, where you're being introduced to this world, but here that's all we get? Something a child would think it's scary?

This kind of horror works perfectly in books, from which the devs seems to have took a lot of inspiration from, since you have to imagine everything and the horror is as scary as your imagination allows. But this is not a book, this is a game, the visuals should have been a key aspect of the experience, but again, unfortunately, the limitations of what the devs could do didn't allow them to deliver a truly scary and unsettling experience.

Second: The story. It's okay at best. 

You have a cult trying to go to a dark magical world. This also works in the first game which was introducing everything, but here? it doesn't go that far. You're looking for Devitt, then you discover more about the cult and then you decide to put an end to it. As i said, it's okay, not bad nor good, just okay. The ending is nothing great as well.

I think the devs wanted to do something big, but didn't have the experience or resources to realize it. Well, at least Blasphemous actually delivers the imagery this game lacks.

Not recommended because this is an okay game on it's own and a horrible sequel.

Season 2 mostly confirmed what I liked about The Last Door in the first place: the story is strong, the atmosphere works best when it is letting you slowly uncover buried truths, and the game is at its best when you are connecting the dots yourself.

The big improvement over Season 1 is that this one at least gives you more control over resolution, which helps a lot. It does not completely solve the visual limitations of the AGI-inspired style on a modern display, but it is a noticeable step up simply because you have options.

Unfortunately, I still think the audio design is a weak point. I understand what the developers were trying to do with sound-driven horror, but the sample quality and lack of proper control still made it feel more clumsy than immersive for me, especially on speakers.

My biggest disappointment was the ending structure. Writing two endings that are almost identical except for who survives did not feel bold or meaningful. It felt more like a token gesture than a genuinely different payoff, and I do not think the character attachment was strong enough to make that choice land.

Even with those issues, I still recommend Season 2. The narrative pull is real, and if you liked Season 1 for the mystery and slow revelation, this delivers more of that while being a little less annoying on the technical side.

[h1]The Last Door: Season 2 - Collector's Edition[/h1]
[h3]Alright Horror Sequel with a Fair Ending[/h3]
[h3]Worth a try if you really want to know how the story ends[/h3]

The Last Door: Season 2 – Collector’s Edition is the sequel and the last entry in the series, closing the story. Like the previous season, it includes four chapters. This time, they are longer and feature a greater number of puzzles. One of the most noticeable improvements on this season is the visual upgrade, the pixel art graphics are cleaner and much easier to read than in the previous game.

[b]Gameplay: Fine point and click horror game with new puzzles and longer chapters
Art: Improved pixel art graphics with a more cleaner appearance 
Music: Still very impressive original soundtrack[/b]

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]
This sequel maintains the same dark atmosphere and the slow paced gameplay style of its predecessor. Sometimes, the puzzles in this game are unclear and less straightforward than before. They now rely less on environmental and tool-based solutions and more on logical deduction. The puzzles are still fun, of course, but they are now somewhat harder to figure out, and it is almost inevitable to get stuck on one or two of them while trying different combinations or approaches.

On one hand, this sequel introduces a new cast of characters with an approach that feels more detective oriented than the mystery or cosmic horror focus of the previous season. The story centers on the search for the previous protagonist and the uncovering of the cult that took him away. On the other hand, the storytelling in this season is much weaker because it focuses so much on side stories that barely connect to the game’s main objective and often feel disconnected from the overall story. 

[h3]Art and World Design[/h3]
The game’s environments and visual assets are more detailed and visually appealing. The sprites are clearer and easier to recognize compared to those of the previous season. Previously, game elements such as notes, keys, or tools were more difficult to distinguish from the environment. This issue was greatly addressed in this season and stands out as one of the most noticeable improvements.
[h3]Music and Sound effects[/h3]
Like its predecessor, the soundtrack remains faithful to the game’s tone and creates a great atmosphere along the chapters. However, the sound design in this entry feels unpolished and with an inconsistent quality. Sometimes, the sound effects are buggy or play too quietly to be noticeable, while at other times they are so loud that they become distracting and even annoying.

[h3]Eight Pixels, No God, Season Two[/h3]

Season Two begins where Season One left off... except now everything’s louder, wetter, and somehow more Catholic. It immediately hands you a cryptic note, a violin stab, and the emotional weight of inheriting a blood curse from someone you’ve never met.

The environments still look like trauma sculpted from geometry homework, but now there are more colors... mostly ones associated with mold. It’s damp everywhere, and you’re never more than a heartbeat away from either a ghost or some bird that’s about to scare the ♥♥♥♥ out of you.

Gameplay remains the classic “click into despair” loop:
You click something.
It ignores you.
You click somewhere else.
Something happens and you’re unclear whether this means progress or punishment.

The puzzles are less “logic” and more “emotional terrorism.”
They’re built around intuitive leaps no functioning adult should be expected to make. You’ll stare at a doorframe for five minutes before realizing the solution was to click a pixel that barely exists. One mistake and you’re back on Google, scrolling through walkthroughs written by people who transcended flesh years ago.

Narratively, Season Two widens the cult...
bigger conspiracies, deeper sadness, and emotional revelations delivered with the enthusiasm of a dying priest.

Characters appear, confess something tragic, and vanish before you can emotionally consent. Everyone has consumption, psychic rot, or a Victorian mental illness that would be instantly cured today with one glass of water and a therapist named Bree.

And somehow...
[b]it works.[/b]

There’s actual heartbreak under all the 144p wallpaper textures.
The sound design feels like a funeral inside a music box.
The ending kind of pisses me off... but still hits harder than anything involving hand-drawn rectangles should.

[b][i]Recommended, especially if you want to be psychologically disciplined by 16-bit Catholic guilt.[/i][/b]

Follow up to the first, it builds on all the things good in the original while furthering the story. Again, a mix of cosmic and gothic horror. This time we follow Jeremiah's therapist, Dr. Wakefield as he searches for his wayward patient, delving into the otherworldly mysteries in the process.

Like the first game, this is all done in a very pixellated style. Very distinct and charming, though also lacking in visual details that can be hit or miss. There are occasions where more visual detail might have served the game better, but for the most part, the art style delivers well.

Carlos Viola continues to not disappoint with the melancholic soundtrack and the rest of the sound adds well to the atmosphere with very few instances where the volume rises for a scare.

Puzzles remained interesting, although it seemed I could readily end up in situations where it wasn't clear what I had to do next. When I eventually found the answer, it became obvious in hindsight in most cases, but there was at least one that might border on being too obtuse. The rest remained comfortable brain teasers.

[spoiler]The story comes to its conclusion and delivers decently on the mysteries it has been building. While there are a lot of elements that remain mysterious, the Lovecraftian aspects make it acceptable.  Though by that same token, one could argue those elements were left underutilized as a result. While the conclusion came together somewhat swiftly, it never felt "too fast."[/spoiler]

[spoiler]It's entirely possible to play this game without the first. They do recap the important bits. But it will likely feel lacking without the first half to compliment it.[/spoiler]

All in all, quite satisfying. If you like these kinds of games or at least a spooky tale of forbidden knowledge, you might enjoy this too.

Supertolles Grusel-Adventure!

Der zweite Teil der Serie ist noch mal besser als der erste Teil und zeitgleich auch der Abschluss dieser Mystery-Geschichte.
Anders als in Teil 1 spielen wir nun die meiste Zeit über einen der beiden Personen, die dem Ganzen auf den Grund gehen und das Verschwinden der Personen untersuchen.

Es gibt wieder 4 Episoden, die nun aber ein ganzen Stück länger sind und sich auch auf mehr Örtlichkeiten erstrecken.
Man bekommt also von der Länge her ein "vollständiges" Adventure, wie man es von größeren Produktionen allgemein gewöhnt ist.

Grafisch setzt man zwar noch immer auf die etwas zu grobe Pixeltechnik, aber man hat das Gefühl, dass da bei der Inzenrierung allgemein noch einmal einer draufgesetzt worden ist.
Aus künstlerischer Sicht ist das Spiel also echt eine Wucht und viele Szenen, Einstellungen und Abläufe sind wirklich toll gemacht.
Das Spielen macht also wirklich auch in Verbindung mit der erneut überwältigend stimmungsvollen Musik sehr viel Spaß und die Geschichte ist eine sehr willkommene Abwechslung und für sich genommen quasi einzigartig.

Die Steam Errungenschaften sind ein guter Anreiz, diese auch erreichen zu wollen.
Dazu sollte man sich aber vorher bei jeder Episode einlesen, worauf man ggf. zu achten hat.
Auch sollte man im Userverzeichnis die automatischen Episodenspielstände zwischenzeitlich immer mal wieder als Kopie ablegen, um möglicherweise später noch einmal darauf zurückgreifen zu können. 
Denn wegen der Länge der Episoden und auch den zahlreichen Zwischensequenzen und Einblendungen etc., kann man da nicht mal eben durchrushen.

Die Schwierigkeit der Rätsel ist gegenüber dem ersten Teil nun ein wenig angehoben worden, auch weil man nun ein wenig mehr Laufwege und Möglichkeiten hat, alles in Allem ist das aber auch für Einsteiger noch gut machbar, also es gibt keine harten Nüsse, wo man sich die Zähne dran ausbeißen sollte.
Weiterhin sollte man darauf achten, dass durch Aktionen woanders etwas passieren kann, und man manchmal einen Auslöser braucht, ehe man etwas machen kann, oder etwas weiter geht.
Nur so kann man halt der Story treu bleiben und gerät in keine Sackgassen.

Mir hat das Spiel wirklich jeden Minute sehr gut gefallen und ich kann es jedem Adventurespieler eindeutig empfehlen, auch denen, die vielleicht eher Grusel- und Horrorspiele in einer 3D-Umgebung mit einer realistischeren Darstellung bevorzugen.

Fazit: kaufen, kaufen, kaufen! :-)

Les énigmes sont plutôt logiques dans l'ensemble, et on ne reste jamais bloqué très longtemps.

Si vous aimez les jeux d'aventure à l'ambiance glauque et mystérieuse et que vous n'êtes pas allergique au pixel art, ce jeu vaut clairement le coup d'oeil.
